# m01-l02 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

The Language of Physics.

Equations are tools physicists use to model observations and make predictions.

Here's our big question for this lesson: how is math helpful to physicists? The short answer is that math is the language physics speaks. Equations are important tools for modeling what we observe and for making predictions. An equation is one way of showing how different measurements are related.

Physicists rely on theories and on experiments with numerical results to back up their conclusions. Try this. If you drop a penny, you can predict that it will fall. Easy! But can you predict how fast it will be going when it hits the ground?

That's harder. Different models of falling objects give different answers about how the speed changes as an object falls, and about what the speed depends on. By measuring how an object really falls, you can compare your data with what each model predicts. That tests the models, so you can pick the best one, or build a brand-new model.

## Slide 2

SI Units, a Shared Language.

SI is the worldwide adaptation of the metric system, built on seven base quantities.

To share results, scientists need units that everyone understands. The worldwide scientific community uses an adaptation of the metric system called the Système International d'Unités, or SI for short. SI uses seven base quantities.

Here they are. Length is measured in meters, symbol m. Mass in kilograms, k g. Time in seconds, s. Temperature in kelvins, capital K. Amount of a substance in moles, m o l. Electric current in amperes, capital A. And luminous intensity, which is about brightness, in candelas, c d.

## Slide 3

Derived Units.

Derived units are formed by combining base units in various ways.

Seven base units can't cover everything on their own, so we combine them. Units built this way are called derived units. Velocity, for example, is measured in meters per second.

Often a derived unit gets its own name. Electric charge is measured in ampere-seconds, and an ampere-second is also called a coulomb, symbol capital C. Same unit, friendlier name.

## Slide 4

Keeping the Standards.

The meter is defined by the distance light travels in a vacuum in one two hundred ninety-nine million, seven hundred ninety-two thousand, four hundred fifty-eighth of a second.

Who decides exactly how long a meter is? SI is regulated by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres, France. In the past, this bureau and the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, in Gaithersburg, Maryland, kept physical samples that the standards were based on.

Now the standards have been redefined in terms of natural phenomena. That change was finished in 2019. Take the meter. In class you'll use metersticks as your standard, but the official meter is defined by light: it's the distance light travels in a vacuum in one two hundred ninety-nine million, seven hundred ninety-two thousand, four hundred fifty-eighth of a second. That's a speedy beam and a very tiny slice of time!

## Slide 5

Prefixes and Powers of Ten.

SI prefixes change a base unit by powers of ten.

One of the handiest things about SI is how easy it is to switch between units. To convert, you just multiply or divide by the right power of ten. Prefixes tell you which power. You already use some in daily life, like milligrams and centimeters.

Going from small to big: femto means ten to the negative fifteenth, as in a femtosecond. Pico is ten to the negative twelfth, as in a picometer. Nano is ten to the negative ninth, a nanometer. Micro, written with the Greek letter mu, is ten to the negative sixth, a microgram. Milli is ten to the negative third, or one thousandth, as in milliamps. Centi is ten to the negative second, one hundredth, a centimeter. And deci is ten to the negative first, one tenth, a deciliter.

Now the big ones. Kilo is ten to the third, or one thousand, as in a kilometer. Mega is ten to the sixth, one million, a megagram. Giga is ten to the ninth, one billion, a gigameter. And tera is ten to the twelfth, one trillion, as in a terahertz.

## Slide 6

Dimensional Analysis.

Dimensional analysis treats units as algebraic quantities that can be canceled.

Physics problems often mean rearranging a formula, or chaining several formulas together. Here's a smart habit: before you calculate anything, write out the equations you plan to use and check that the answer will come out in the units you expect.

Say you're finding a car's speed, and your setup gives units of seconds per meter, or meters per second squared. Stop! You've made an error somewhere. Treating units as algebra, so they can cancel, is called dimensional analysis.

One honest warning: getting the right units doesn't guarantee the right answer. But if your units come out wrong, you know for sure that something went wrong.

## Slide 7

Conversion Factors.

A conversion factor is a multiplier equal to one.

Dimensional analysis also helps you choose conversion factors. A conversion factor is a multiplier equal to one, so it changes the units without changing the actual amount.

Because one kilogram equals one thousand grams, you can build two conversion factors: one kilogram over one thousand grams, and one thousand grams over one kilogram. Both equal one. Pick the one that makes your starting units cancel.

Let's convert 1.34 kilograms to grams. Multiply 1.34 kilograms by one thousand grams over one kilogram. The kilograms cancel, and you get 1340 grams.

Sometimes you chain conversions. To change 43 kilometers per hour into meters per second, multiply 43 kilometers per hour by one thousand meters over one kilometer, then by one hour over 60 minutes, then by one minute over 60 seconds. Kilometers, hours, and minutes all cancel, leaving 12 meters per second.

## Slide 8

Significant Figures.

Significant figures are the valid digits in a measurement.

Suppose you measure a pen, and its end lands just past the 138 millimeter mark on the ruler. You estimate it's one tenth of a millimeter past that last tick, so you record 138.1 millimeters.

That measurement has four valid digits. The first three are certain, and the last one is your estimate, so it's uncertain. The valid digits in a measurement are called significant figures. The last digit of any measurement is always the uncertain one, and every nonzero digit in a measurement is significant.

## Slide 9

Are All Zeros Significant?

Zeros that only locate the decimal point are not significant.

Zeros are tricky. Are they all significant? Nope! In the measurement 0.0860 meters, the first two zeros only show where the decimal point goes, so they aren't significant. But that last zero is the estimated digit, so it is significant.

Now look at 172,000 meters. That could have three, four, five, or six significant figures. There's no way to tell! This is one reason scientists use scientific notation. Written as 1.7200 times ten to the fifth meters, it clearly has five significant figures.

## Slide 10

Doing Math with Significant Figures.

A result can never be more precise than the least-precise measurement.

When you do arithmetic with measurements, remember one rule: your answer can never be more precise than your least-precise measurement.

To add or subtract, do the math first, then round to match the least-precise value. For example, 3.86 meters plus 2.4 meters equals 6.3 meters, not 6.26 meters, because the least-precise measurement only goes to the tenth of a meter.

To multiply or divide, do the math first, then round to the same number of significant figures as the least-precise measurement. For example, 409.2 kilometers divided by 11.4 liters equals 35.9 kilometers per liter, because the least-precise measurement has three significant figures. Watch your calculator, too. Some show extra digits, and others round at different points, so always record your answer with the correct number of digits.

## Slide 11

Example Problem 1, Using Distance and Time to Find Speed.

Example problems are solved in three steps: analyze and sketch, solve for the unknown, evaluate the answer.

Most problems in this course need a strategy, so every example problem uses a three-step process. Let's try one. A car travels 434 kilometers in 4.5 hours. What is its average speed?

Step one: analyze and sketch the problem. The car's speed is unknown. We know the distance, 434 kilometers, and the time, 4.5 hours. We'll use the relationship among speed, distance, and time.

Step two: solve for the unknown. Distance equals speed times time. Solve that for speed: speed equals distance divided by time. Substitute 434 kilometers for distance and 4.5 hours for time. Calculate, and include the units: the calculator shows 96.44 kilometers per hour. The time, 4.5 hours, has only two significant figures, so we round to 96 kilometers per hour. Note: the original example gave 96.4 kilometers per hour; the correct answer is 96 kilometers per hour because our answer can't be more precise than the least-precise measurement.

Step three: evaluate the answer. First, check the units: kilometers divided by hours gives kilometers per hour, a speed unit. Good. Next, estimate: 434 kilometers is about 400, and 4.5 hours is about 4, so the speed should be about 100 kilometers per hour. Our answer of 96 is close to that. Finally, ask if it makes sense: 96 kilometers per hour is a normal highway speed for a car. So the answer is reasonable.
